title: Research Bite #18: The Role of Rewards in Motivation—Beyond Dichotomies
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #18 covers Lisa Bardach and Kou Murayama's "The Role of Rewards in Motivation -- Beyond Dichotomies," which challenges the standard classroom-lore claim that extrinsic rewards (stickers, grades, prizes) always undermine intrinsic motivation. The authors propose a "motivation transformation" model in which extrinsic rewards can act as an entry point that pulls an unmotivated learner into a task, after which the learner may come to experience the activity's internal rewards and shift toward genuine intrinsic interest. Crucially, they argue the relationship is dynamic rather than fixed: rewards that helped launch engagement can become counterproductive if they remain too prominent once intrinsic motivation has taken hold, crowding out the learner's developing enjoyment of the work itself. The paper draws on multiple motivational frameworks to argue for personalized, time-sensitive reward use rather than a blanket "rewards are bad" or "rewards are good" rule. For teachers, the practical message is to use extrinsic incentives deliberately to start the engagement cycle, to reward effort rather than only ability or outcome, and to watch for the point at which rewards should be withdrawn or made less salient so they don't interrupt a student's transition to intrinsic motivation.
points: The "motivation transformation" model reframes the rewards debate: extrinsic incentives aren't inherently corrosive, they're an entry point that can seed intrinsic motivation if timed correctly.
The risk isn't using rewards, it's leaving them too prominent for too long once a student's intrinsic motivation has started to develop, which can crowd out and disrupt that emerging engagement.
Rewarding effort rather than ability or raw achievement increases the intrinsic value students attach to the mental labor itself, per the authors.
The paper's call for personalized reward systems -- tailored to a student's stage of knowledge acquisition and the specific task -- pushes back against one-size-fits-all reward or no-reward policies.
quotes: This research paper examines the complex relationship between extrinsic rewards (like gold stars or money) and intrinsic motivation (enjoyment of learning). The authors challenge the traditional view that extrinsic rewards always undermine intrinsic motivation, proposing a “motivation transformation” model.

This model suggests that extrinsic rewards can serve as an “entry point” to engage initially unmotivated learners, potentially leading to intrinsic motivation as they experience the internal rewards of learning.
However, the authors caution that once intrinsic motivation is established, excessive extrinsic rewards can disrupt this process, leading to decreased engagement.

Once students are engaged in a positive feedback loop of learning, teachers should be cautious about making extrinsic rewards too prominent, as they can interrupt the learning process and harm long-term engagement.
Extrinsic rewards should not be stopped too early, but they also shouldn’t be prolonged for too long. They can be useful for sustaining long-term engagement, especially when students face challenges.

Teachers should reward students for their effort, not just their abilities or achievements. Rewarding effort can increase the intrinsic value of mental labor. Extrinsic rewards can “train” effortful engagement.
